FOR RELEASE OCTOBER 14, 2026 Online Community and Connection in America Nearly 4 in 10 U.S. adults – including about half of those 18 to 29 – are part of an online community BY Colleen McClain, Jeffrey Gottfried, Eugenie Park, Michelle Faverio, Olivia Sidoti and Monica Anderson FOR MEDIA OR OTHER INQUIRIES: Colleen McClain, Senior Researcher Jeffrey Gottfried, Associate Director, Internet and Technology Research Monica Anderson, Director, Internet and Technology Research Haley Nolan, Communications Manager 202.419.4372 www.pewresearch.org RECOMMENDED CITATION Pew Research Center, October 2026, “Online Community and Connection in America”

1 PEW RESEARCH CENTER www.pewresearch.org About the Pew-Knight Initiative The Pew-Knight Initiative supports new research on how Americans absorb civic information, form beliefs and identities, and engage in their communities. Pew Research Center is a nonpartisan, nonadvocacy fact tank that informs the public about the issues, attitudes and trends shaping the world. Knight Foundation is a social investor committed to supporting informed and engaged communities. © Pew Research Center 2026

# Page 3^page=3
2 PEW RESEARCH CENTER www.pewresearch.org About this research This report from the Pew-Knight Initiative focuses on online community and connection today. It looks at who’s part of online communities, where they form, what they’re built around, why people go to them – and why some people leave. It also examines what people think the internet is doing to connection overall. Why we did this The Center conducts research to inform the public, journalists and decision-makers. We’ve long studied what online connection looks like for Americans. At a time when fewer than half of Americans are highly satisfied with their social life – or with the quality of life in their local community – it’s important to understand the role online communities play, good and bad. Learn more about Pew Research Center. How we did this We surveyed 9,750 U.S. adults from May 26 to June 1, 2026. Everyone who took part in this survey is a member of the Center’s American Trends Panel. The survey represents the views of the full U.S. adult population. Here are the survey questions used for this report, the detailed responses and the methodology. This is a Pew Research Center report from the Pew-Knight Initiative, a research program funded jointly by The Pew Charitable Trusts and the John S. and James L. Knight Foundation. Find related reports online at https://www.pewresearch.org/pew-knight/.

# Page 4^page=4
3 PEW RESEARCH CENTER www.pewresearch.org Online Community and Connection in America Nearly 4 in 10 U.S. adults – including about half of those 18 to 29 – are part of an online community At a time when many are worrying about fraying social ties and rising loneliness, some Americans are finding community online. A new Pew Research Center survey from the Pew-Knight Initiative finds that nearly four- in-ten U.S. adults are part of an online community – and that share rises to about half among young adults. For some, these communities are deeply valuable parts of their lives. They widely offer information, advice or experiences people say they could only get online. Still, these benefits sit alongside doubts about making genuine connections online. About half of Americans question whether online relationships can be as Nearly 4 in 10 Americans are part of online communities – and this is higher for young adults % of U.S. adults who say they are part of online communities Note: For details on how we asked about being part of online communities, refer to the topline. Source: Pew Research Center survey of U.S. adults conducted May 26-June 1, 2026. “Online Community and Connection in America” PEW-KNIGHT INITIATIVE Key findings: ▪ 48% of young adults are part of online communities, outpacing older adults. ▪ These communities often offer unique value: For many, their go-to space is something they can only get online. ▪ Most go to them for information, fun or advice. Fewer go to them for acceptance or meeting people. ▪ Many think politics doesn’t belong in the space they visit most – 54% say this. ▪ Not everyone’s sold on online connection. About half of adults say it’s not as meaningful as in-person relationships. ▪ The most common reason people leave online communities? # Page 5^page=5
4 PEW RESEARCH CENTER www.pewresearch.org meaningful as those formed in person. Fewer – 34% – think they can be just as meaningful. There’s an age divide on this topic as well. Adults under 30 are far more likely than those ages 65 and older to say online relationships can be just as meaningful as in-person ones (54% vs. 14%). How did we study online community? Our questions asked about feeling part of a community online. We wanted to capture a wide range of spaces and experiences that someone might consider as online community. Here’s how we explained the topic further: By this, we mean people connecting with others online, such as by joining or feeling part of a group or doing things together. This could happen in places like social media, online discussion forums, by emailing or messaging with a group, or in video games online. Follow-up questions focused on the community people spend the most time in – we call this their most- visited online community.

# Page 6^page=6
5 PEW RESEARCH CENTER www.pewresearch.org Where online communities form and what they’re about More than two decades after the Center studied online communities in 2001, these spaces still vary in where they form, what they offer and who turns to them. It’s most common to find online community on social media. About a quarter of Americans are part of an online community on social media sites or apps. Discussion forums come next – 15% are part of an online community in places like Reddit, Nextdoor or Discord. Fewer are part of an online community on video sites like YouTube and Twitch, in video games online, or on messaging apps. And 5% are part of one on sites or apps for people who share a hobby – like Goodreads for reading, Strava for running, Ravelry for knitting or Letterboxd for movies. Social media top the list of where people find community online % of U.S. adults who say they are part of an online community in the following places Note: For details on how we asked about being part of online communities, as well as the share who said they were part of online communities elsewhere, refer to the topline. Source: Pew Research Center survey of U.S. adults conducted May 26-June 1, 2026. “Online Community and Connection in America” PEW-KNIGHT INITIATIVE

# Page 7^page=7
6 PEW RESEARCH CENTER www.pewresearch.org When it comes to what these communities focus on: Hobbies and local area top the list. About one-in-five Americans say they are part of an online community related to each. Roughly one-in-ten adults say they’re in one about topics like movies, books or TV shows; video games; or their work or profession. A similar share says they’re in fan communities of any kind. And while politics can come up in a range of places, 8% of Americans are in an online community specifically related to politics or political issues. Read more about what people think of politics in online communities. Age, again, is an important factor: Young adults are more likely than all other groups to be part of several kinds of communities. For example, that’s true for online communities about video games; beauty or fashion; movies, books or TV shows; hobbies; and fan communities. Gaming has one of the biggest gaps. About a quarter of adults under 30 (27%) are part of one about video games. This drops to 16% of those in their 30s and 40s and 4% of those 50 and older. Participation also varies by other factors. Some examples are: It’s most common to be part of online communities about hobbies, local area % of U.S. adults who say they are part of the following kinds of online communities Note: The gender item was specific to how people described themselves. # Page 8^page=8
7 PEW RESEARCH CENTER www.pewresearch.org ▪ Gender: 15% of women are part of an online community specifically for women, largely driven by women under 50; 5% of men say they’re in one specifically for men. ▪ Being a parent: 17% of parents with a child under 18 say they’re part of an online community about parenting. Moms are more likely than dads to say so (21% vs. 11%). ▪ Race and ethnicity: Roughly one-in-five Black adults (17%) are part of a community related to race and ethnicity. About one-in-ten Asian or Hispanic adults say this and 2% of White adults. For more on who’s part of an online community in general, go to the appendix. Do people find value in online communities? Online communities are widely seen as unique spaces and can add deeply to people’s lives. About a quarter of those in online communities say these places are highly valuable to them. A larger share – about four-in-ten – finds some value there. Together, about seven-in-ten say these spaces add something to their lives. Still, 29% of those who are part of online communities say they bring little to no value. Both younger and older adults tend to find at least some value in these places. But adults under 50 in them are more likely to say they add deeply to their lives, compared with older adults (32% vs. 20%). # Page 9^page=9
8 PEW RESEARCH CENTER www.pewresearch.org What are people taking away from the communities they go to most ? It’s common to be part of multiple online communities. In fact, 85% of those in online communities are part of more than one. To better understand people’s experiences, we asked some questions about the one they visit most often. First, we asked people to tell us in a few words what the focus of their most-visited community is. These covered a vast array of topics, such as a specific hobby, neighborhood, musical group, medical condition or identity, for example. Other communities focused on connecting and talking with others. # Page 11^page=11
10 PEW RESEARCH CENTER www.pewresearch.org Wh at motivates people to turn to online communit ies ? People seek out online communities for a variety of reasons, but there are three near the top of our list: to stay informed, for fun or to get advice or recommendations. About eight-in-ten or more say they go to their most-visited community for each of these. This includes more than half who cite information and fun as major reasons. Smaller shares – though still majorities – say a major or minor reason they visit their go-to space is to share their thoughts or get support. Just over half also say they go there because they feel accepted. And fewer say it’s to meet new people or for the drama. Information and fun are among the top reasons people go to online communities Among U.S. adults in online communities, % who say each of the following is a __ reason they go to their most-visited community Note: For details on how we asked about being part of online communities, refer to the topline. Those who did not answer or said “not a reason” are not shown. Source: Pew Research Center survey of U.S. adults conducted May 26-June 1, 2026. “Online Community and Connection in America” PEW-KNIGHT INITIATIVE

# Page 12^page=12
11 PEW RESEARCH CENTER www.pewresearch.org Young adults are more likely than older age groups to turn to online communities because they feel accepted or to meet new people – but also for the drama. For example, when asked about their most-visited online community, roughly six-in-ten under 30 say they go there to meet new people. Among those in their 30s and 40s, fewer (46%) say the same. And this share drops further for those 50 and older. The pattern is similar for seeing if there’s drama or feeling accepted. But those in their 30s and 40s are just as likely as young adults to go to these places for support, advice or recommendations, or to share their thoughts. And on some reasons – like staying informed – there is little difference by age. Most across groups say this is a motivator. Connection in online communities There are many ways online communities can bring value to people’s lives. All told, meeting people is fairly low on the list of motivators. We see that reflected in people’s feelings, too. Major/minor reason are combined. Statistically significant differences in bold. Difference values shown are based on subtracting the rounded numbers in the chart. Those who did not answer or said “not a reason” are not shown. Source: Pew Research Center survey of U.S. adults conducted May 26-June 1, 2026. “Online Community and Connection in America” PEW-KNIGHT INITIATIVE

# Page 13^page=13
12 PEW RESEARCH CENTER www.pewresearch.org About one-in-five say they feel extremely or very close to others in these spaces, and an additional 37% feel somewhat close. But nearly half don’t feel very close to others in their most-visited community. That includes 14% who don’t feel close at all. People tend to start fresh in these spaces. Most (68%) knew very few or none of the people there before joining. And it’s less common to feel close to others if you knew few people starting out. Of those who knew very few or no one, about one-in-ten say they feel extremely or very close to people there today. Even so, these spaces start conversations that are often part of members’ daily lives. The vast majority of those in online communities – 74% – say they ever post or share in the one they visit most. And nearly six-in-ten (56%) say they go to their most-visited community every day. That’s one-in- five U.S. adults overall who say they’re in an online community daily. When asked about their most-visited space, about a third say that it has in-person gatherings, too. # Page 15^page=15
14 PEW RESEARCH CENTER www.pewresearch.org Is online connection meaningful? When we ask Americans for their take on online relationships more broadly – regardless of if they’re in an online community or not – we find many doubt the value of online connection. About half of Americans overall say personal relationships formed online are not as meaningful as in-person ones. About one-third say they can be just as meaningful, while 20% aren’t sure. But views on this issue vary a lot by age. Adults under 30 are the only age group in which more say online relationships can be just as meaningful, than say they don’t measure up. And while a quarter of those who are not in an online community find digital connection on par with in-person, this rises to 48% of those who are in one. Younger adults are more likely to say online relationships are just as meaningful as in-person ones % of U.S. adults who say in general, they think personal relationships that people form online __ as in-person relationships Note: Those who did not answer are not shown. # Page 16^page=16
15 PEW RESEARCH CENTER www.pewresearch.org Skepticism also shows up in broader views of the internet’s role in how people relate to each other. More Americans say the internet tends to drive people apart, than think it tends to bring them together (31% vs. 11%). But by far the largest share – 58% – thinks the internet does both about equally. Unlike when we ask about relationships, there’s little difference by age here. Across groups, more say the internet divides than unites. And the largest shares in each group say it does both. These tensions can be felt in online communities, too. The ones people visit most often are widely viewed as respectful. Still, tone can cross a line: Too much arguing is among the reasons why people leave online communities, though not the most common one. Read more about who has left an online community – and why. More say the internet divides than connects. Many think it does both % of U.S. adults who say the internet does more to … Note: The 1% who did not answer are not shown. Source: Pew Research Center survey of U.S. adults conducted May 26-June 1, 2026. “Online Community and Connection in America” PEW-KNIGHT INITIATIVE Drive people apart 31 11 Bring people together Both about equally 58

# Page 17^page=17
16 PEW RESEARCH CENTER www.pewresearch.org Online Communities Rarely Focus on Politics, and Many Say It Should Stay That Way Politics can find a way into online communities, whether they are focused on politics or built around other topics from neighborhoods to parenting. But a new Pew Research Center survey from the Pew-Knight Initiative finds that politics is not a big driver of conversation in the online communities people visit most. And a majority don’t think politics should be there. Still, party and ideology can play a role. Liberal Democrats tend to differ from other groups in how they feel about politics in these spaces, and what kinds of communities they’re part of broadly. Among people who are part of one, about three-in-ten say there’s at least some political discussion in the online community they visit most often. This includes 7% who say it makes up all or most of the discussion. But most – 71% – say they see little to no political content in their go-to community. This is part of a broader survey of U.S. adults, conducted May 26-June 1, 2026. The <1% who did not answer are not shown. Source: Pew Research Center survey of U.S. adults conducted May 26-June 1, 2026. “Online Community and Connection in America” PEW-KNIGHT INITIATIVE

# Page 18^page=18
17 PEW RESEARCH CENTER www.pewresearch.org Many say politics does not belong in these spaces People commonly say they don’t want to see politics in their go-to communities. In fact, a majority (54%) of those in an online community say political discussion does not belong in the one they visit most often. A much smaller share – a quarter – says politics does belong there, and 21% aren’t sure. We’ve seen similar themes in our work on social media. For example, on two of the four platforms we studied in a 2024 survey, majorities of users who keep politics out of their posts said it’s because politics doesn’t belong there. Some Americans who’ve left an online community say it was due to too much politics (44% of those who’ve left one). Go to “About a Third of Americans Have Left an Online Community” to read more. # Page 19^page=19
18 PEW RESEARCH CENTER www.pewresearch.org Is the political content people see new or more of the same? People commonly say the online community they visit most has unique value – it’s something they can’t find elsewhere. But political discussion in these communities isn’t always unique to the space it’s in. More often than not, political content reflects what people are already getting elsewhere. At the same time, it’s most commonly a diversity of viewpoints, rather than just what people agree with. The political information people see in these spaces is more often familiar than not. About a quarter of those in online communities say the political information they see in their most-visited community is mostly what they’ve seen elsewhere. Just 5% say it’s mostly new to them. And about a quarter say it’s about equally new and familiar. People there are also more likely to say they see things they mostly agree with than disagree (19% vs. 6%). Still, it’s more common to see a roughly equal mix of political content you agree and disagree with. About three-in-ten in online communities say this. # Page 20^page=20
19 PEW RESEARCH CENTER www.pewresearch.org Liberal Democrats stand out for how they experience politics in online communities When the focus turns to politics in these spaces, liberal Democrats differ from other groups in several ways. (Republicans and Democrats include independents who lean toward each party.) Among those in online communities: Liberal Democrats are most likely to say politics belongs in the communities they visit most, at 37%. A similar share (43%) says it doesn’t – but that view is higher in other partisan and ideological groups. Liberal Democrats are also more likely to say they see like-minded political posts and things that reflect what they get elsewhere. For instance, about a third of liberal Democrats say they mostly agree with what they see, far higher than other groups. That said, roughly another quarter of liberal Democrats say they see a mix of political information that they agree and disagree with. Liberal Democrats more likely to be part of political online communities Beyond the online communities Americans visit most often, we wanted to understand the broader landscape of what spaces people are part of. # Page 22^page=22
21 PEW RESEARCH CENTER www.pewresearch.org About a Third of Americans Have Left an Online Community Online communities can draw people in with shared interests, support or a sense of belonging. But for some Americans, these spaces aren’t forever, according to a new Pew Research Center survey from the Pew-Knight Initiative. About a third of U.S. adults say they have ever left an online community, according to the survey conducted May 26-June 1, 2026. This includes both some who currently are in an online community and some who are not. When people move on from them, they cite a range of reasons – but declining interest is a big one. # Page 23^page=23
22 PEW RESEARCH CENTER www.pewresearch.org Losing interest is the most common reason people cite for leaving an online community. More than eight- in-ten who’ve left one say this, and it’s the only reason a majority name as a major factor for stepping away. Declining quality and life changes are also reasons that majorities say contribute in at least a minor way to why they’ve left. Toxicity is another factor: 57% of those who’ve left cite too much arguing. And 43% say it’s because people were being harassed.1 Others stepped away because of politics. Just over four-in- ten say they left an online community because politics was brought up too much. And as Americans continue to grapple with screen time, 37% left because they were spending too much time there. By age Younger adults are more likely to be part of online communities. But adults under 50 are also more likely to have left one, compared with older adults. ▪ 44% of adults under 30 have left an online community. 1 Previous Center studies show that substantial shares of both adults and teenagers experience online harassment and cyberbullying. Loss of interest and declining quality are common reasons why people leave online communities. The American Trends Panel survey methodology Overview Data in this report comes from Wave 194 of the American Trends Panel (ATP), Pew Research Center’s nationally representative panel of randomly selected U.S. adults. The survey was conducted from May 26 to June 1, 2026. A total of 9,750 panelists responded out of 11,184 who were sampled, for a survey-level response rate of 87%. The cumulative response rate accounting for nonresponse to the recruitment surveys and attrition is 3%. The break-off rate among panelists who logged on to the survey and completed at least one item is less than 1%. The margin of sampling error for the full sample of 9,750 respondents is plus or minus 1.4 percentage points. SSRS conducted the survey for Pew Research Center via online (n=9,464) and live telephone (n=286) interviewing. Interviews were conducted in both English and Spanish. To learn more about the ATP, read “About the American Trends Panel.” Panel recruitment Since 2018, the ATP has used address-based sampling (ABS) for recruitment. A study cover letter and a pre-incentive are mailed to a stratified, random sample of households selected from the U.S. Postal Service’s Computerized Delivery Sequence File. This Postal Service file has been estimated to cover 90% to 98% of the population.2 Within each sampled household, the adult with the next birthday is selected to participate. Other details of the ABS recruitment protocol have changed over time but are available upon request.3 Prior to 2018, the ATP was recruited using landline and cellphone random-digit-dial surveys administered in English and Spanish. A national sample of U.S. adults has been recruited to the ATP approximately once per year since 2014. In some years, the recruitment has included additional efforts (known as an “oversample”) 2 AAPOR Task Force on Address-based Sampling. 2016. “AAPOR Report: Address-based Sampling.” 3 Email pewsurveys@pewresearch.org.

For example, Hispanic adults, Black adults and Asian adults were oversampled in 2019, 2022 and 2023, respectively. Sample design The overall target population for this survey was noninstitutionalized persons ages 18 and older living in the United States. All active panel members were invited to participate in this wave. Questionnaire development and testing The questionnaire was developed by Pew Research Center in consultation with SSRS. The web program used for online respondents was rigorously tested on both PC and mobile devices by the SSRS project team and Pew Research Center researchers. The SSRS project team also populated test data that was analyzed in SPSS to ensure the logic and randomizations were working as intended before launching the survey. Incentives All respondents were offered a post-paid incentive for their participation. Respondents could choose to receive the post-paid incentive in the form of a check or gift code to Amazon.com, Target.com or Walmart.com. Incentive amounts ranged from $5 to $20 depending on whether the respondent belongs to a part of the population that is harder or easier to reach. Differential incentive amounts were designed to increase panel survey participation among groups that traditionally have low survey response propensities. Data collection protocol The data collection field period for this survey was May 26 to June 1, 2026. Surveys were conducted via self-administered web survey or by live telephone interviewing. For panelists who take surveys online:4 Postcard notifications were mailed to a subset on May 26.5 Survey invitations were sent out in two separate launches: soft launch and full launch. Sixty panelists were included in the soft launch, which began with an initial invitation sent on May 26. All remaining English- and Spanish-speaking sampled online panelists were included in the full launch and were sent an invitation on May 27. 4 The ATP does not use routers or chains in any part of its online data collection protocol, nor are they used to direct respondents to additional surveys. 5 Postcard notifications for web panelists are sent to 1) panelists who were recruited within the last two years and 2) panelists recruited prior to the last two years who opt to continue receiving postcard notifications.

35 PEW RESEARCH CENTER www.pewresearch.org Open -end coding methodology Open-ended responses to the question about the focus of people’s most-visited online community were coded using AI-assisted text classification. Human researchers reviewed, validated and, where necessary, corrected AI-generated codes prior to analysis. Center researchers developed a coding scheme using a model-assisted codebook development process that integrated human interpretation with unsupervised machine learning. First, researchers reviewed a randomly selected pilot sample of responses to independently identify key themes. In parallel, we used an unsupervised theme-discovery approach – based on sparse autoencoders and LLM-based interpretation – to generate candidate themes, using the HypotheSAEs method developed by Movva et al. (2025).6 This process included several steps: 1. We converted each open-ended response into a numerical representation that captures its meaning, using an embedding model (OpenAI’s text-embedding-3-small). 2. We then fit a sparse autoencoder to those representations – essentially training a model to describe every response using a limited set of features. The model ends up learning common themes corresponding to ideas that recur across many responses. 3. We identified a list of the most common themes, examined the responses that exemplified each most strongly, and used a large language model (GPT-5.2) to summarize the common thread of the category. 4. Researchers then reviewed and revised the set of candidate categories, combining researcher and LLM insights to create an initial codebook. We gave the codebook to a large language model (GPT-5.2) alongside a prompt instructing the model to use it to code the open-ended responses with the category that most strongly applied or the first referenced if multiple were mentioned. We validated the model’s performance against a sample of responses that researchers coded by hand. We drew a stratified sample of 210 responses to ensure that every category, including rare ones, was represented, supplemented by a set of randomly selected responses. Both the LLM and the human coders coded each response for the single best-fit label. Human coders worked from the same codebook and were not shown the automated codes. Agreement was measured using standard metrics for single-label classification. We also reviewed cases where the automated and human coding disagreed to understand these patterns and to inform revisions to the coding rules. 6 Movva, Rajiv, Kenny Peng, Nikhil Garg, Jon Kleinberg, and Emma Pierson. 2025. “Sparse autoencoders for hypothesis generation.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2502.04382

36 PEW RESEARCH CENTER www.pewresearch.org After minor adjustments to the codebook, the automated coding achieved a micro-averaged F1 score of 0.86. Once validated, the LLM used the codebook to categorize all 3,635 responses. For each answer, the model followed a fixed procedure: The model read the response and selected exactly one code that fit the best; if multiple groups were mentioned in the response, it coded for the first one mentioned. The LLM only coded a response with the “Other” category if no other codable groups were present. It coded any blank, gibberish or nonsensical answers as “No answer.” A set of deterministic rules were applied afterward to enforce the codebook’s logic.
